title: Sequence or use case? See the difference.
intro: Use-case diagrams describe the goals a system supports and the external roles involved. Sequence diagrams follow the messages exchanged during one scenario, in time order.
scopeNote: Supplementary explanation requested for studying. The professor’s review establishes exam scope; this lesson does not imply that sequence diagrams are confirmed midterm questions.

comparison.useCase: Who uses the system, and what goals does it support?
comparison.sequence: Who sends which message to whom, and in what order?

comparison.useCase: Actors, system boundary, use-case ovals, associations, include, extend, generalization.
comparison.sequence: Participants, lifelines, activation bars, messages, returns, and guarded alternatives.

comparison.useCase: Connections describe participation and relationships. They do not establish chronological order.
comparison.sequence: Read messages from top to bottom to follow the interaction order.

comparison.useCase: Airline Support System: check in, check baggage, boarding, and change flight.
comparison.sequence: ATM withdrawal: the user, ATM, and bank system exchange messages.

bridge: A hypothetical ATM use-case overview could name “Withdraw cash.” The sequence diagram then explains how one withdrawal unfolds. This bridge is an app-authored comparison; the supplied ATM solution is a sequence diagram.

sequence.title: ATM withdrawal: follow the messages
sequence.subtitle: ATM means automated teller machine. PIN means personal identification number. Client is the user; : ATM and bankSystem : BankSystem are the other participants.

messages.label: Insert a card
messages.explanation: The user starts the interaction by inserting a card into the ATM.

messages.label: Verify the card
messages.explanation: A self-call shows the ATM doing work on its own lifeline.

messages.label: Enter card PIN
messages.explanation: The user supplies the PIN. This is a new message, later than inserting the card.

messages.label: Check PIN
messages.explanation: The ATM checks the PIN; the source draws this as another self-call.

messages.label: Choose amount to withdraw
messages.explanation: The user specifies the requested withdrawal amount.

messages.label: Check funds (requestedAmount)
messages.explanation: The ATM asks the bank system to check the client’s funds for the requested amount.

branches.label: Transaction approved
branches.explanation: The bank returns permission. The ATM gives money and returns the card.

branches.label: Transaction rejected
branches.explanation: The bank returns rejection. The ATM shows rejection details and returns the card.

branches.label: Card blocked
branches.explanation: The bank reports a blocked card. The ATM keeps the card and displays blocking information.

notation: Dashed vertical lifelines represent participants over time; activation bars indicate periods of activity.
Solid arrows are messages; the source’s dashed horizontal arrows show bank responses.
An arrow that loops back to the same lifeline is a self-call.
The alt frame contains guarded alternatives. Approved, rejected, and blocked-card paths are alternatives, not three successive stages. Only the chosen path is highlighted in this walkthrough.

airline.title: Airline Support System: actors and goals
airline.subtitle: Use cases sit inside the Airline Support System boundary. Actors sit outside it. TSA means Transportation Security Administration; an actor can be a person or an external system.

explorations.label: Check in and its variants
explorations.explanation: Passenger and check-in representative participate in Check in. Mobile, Online, and Terminal check in specialize the general Check in use case; hollow triangles point toward Check in. These are alternative ways to check in, not three mandatory include relationships. In the requested model, Check in includes Issue boarding pass.

explorations.label: Check baggage
explorations.explanation: Passenger and check-in representative participate in Check baggage. Baggage management system is an external system actor connected to this goal, demonstrating that actors need not be people.

explorations.label: Issue boarding pass and security
explorations.explanation: Passenger receives a boarding pass, with the check-in representative participating in issuing it. The requested model has Check in include Issue boarding pass, and Issue boarding pass include Security check. TSA participates in Security check. Include arrows point toward the required included behavior.

explorations.label: Boarding
explorations.explanation: Boarding is a passenger goal. The instructor source also shows Boarding include Issue boarding pass. This is a modeled dependency on included behavior, not a timeline saying when the passenger boards.

explorations.label: Change flight
explorations.explanation: Passenger can Change flight; the source also connects the check-in representative. Ordinary actor associations are undirected and indicate participation.

airline.sourceNote: Annotated redraw of your requested model. The handwritten instructor solution points Issue boarding pass → Check in and Security check → Issue boarding pass. Your requested inclusion semantics use Check in → Issue boarding pass and Issue boarding pass → Security check. The redraw follows your model and labels these differences rather than silently changing the original. These are class-exercise assumptions, not a description of actual airline or TSA operations.

checks.prompt: Which diagram answers “Who can check in or change a flight?”
checks.explanation: A use-case diagram connects actors to supported user goals.

checks.prompt: In the ATM example, what happens after the user chooses an amount?
choices: The ATM asks the bank system to check funds
The three alternative outcomes occur one after another
The user inserts a card for the first time
checks.explanation: Messages run top to bottom: the amount is chosen before the ATM requests a funds check.

checks.prompt: What does the ATM alt frame mean?
checks.explanation: Approval, rejection, and a blocked card are alternative outcomes, not consecutive steps.

checks.prompt: Why is the baggage management system an actor?
choices: Only a human may be an actor
It is an external system interacting with the Airline Support System
It is an internal use-case oval
checks.explanation: An actor is an external interacting role, including an external system.

checks.prompt: In your requested model, which way does the Check in include arrow point?
checks.explanation: Include points from the including use case to its included behavior. The handwritten source reverses this relationship; the annotated redraw makes the requested semantics explicit.

checks.prompt: How do Mobile, Online, and Terminal check in relate to Check in?
choices: All three are required steps, connected by include
They are specializations, with hollow triangles pointing to Check in
checks.explanation: Generalization points from a specialized use case toward the general use case. It does not impose a chronological order.
